title: NextMed GLP-1 telehealth: fake before/after testimonials, unsubstantiated '53 lbs average' claims, buried drug-cost disclaimer
company: Southern Health Solutions, Inc. d/b/a Next Medical and NextMed
ad_content:
$99 Ozempic Buy Now - No Diet or Exercise Required
Members Lose 53+ lbs Without Diet or Exercise.
NextMed offers new FDA approved weight-loss medications like Ozempic and Wegovy
First month only $99, lose 23% body weight in ’23!
Personalized, Doctor-Backed Semaglutide
Our members lose over 53 lbs on average.
Over the course of the program, eligible customers can expect to lose up to an average of 23% of body weight. Our average member has a starting weight of 230 pounds and can lose 53 pounds at 23% weight loss.
Monthly prescription to a GLP-1a medication for weight-loss…
Chastity - Lost 38lbs: I found Next Medical 5 months ago, and have already gotten down to my lowest weight since I was a teenager. My doctor has helped me get into the best shape of my life!
Becky - Lost 54lbs: The hardest part of losing weight is getting started. I finally decided I wanted to get into shape in February, and signed up with Next Medical. I have already lost a lot of weight on Ozempic, and my husband loves it!
Frank - Lost 105lbs: NextMed’s program really was a lifesaver for me. Wegovy helped me get to my lowest weight in five years. Great program.

expected_findings.claim: I found Next Medical 5 months ago, and have already gotten down to my lowest weight since I was a teenager. My doctor has helped me get into the best shape of my life!
expected_findings.rule: FTC Act §§5(a) and 12 [15 U.S.C. 45(a), 52] — Count III, False and Misleading Testimonials and Endorsements

expected_findings.claim: NextMed’s program really was a lifesaver for me. Wegovy helped me get to my lowest weight in five years. Great program.
expected_findings.rule: FTC Act §§5(a) and 12 [15 U.S.C. 45(a), 52] — Count III, False and Misleading Testimonials and Endorsements

expected_findings.claim: Our members lose over 53 lbs on average.
expected_findings.rule: FTC Act §§5(a) and 12 [15 U.S.C. 45(a), 52] — Count II, Unsubstantiated Weight Loss Claims

expected_findings.claim: Members Lose 53+ lbs Without Diet or Exercise.
expected_findings.rule: FTC Act §§5(a) and 12 [15 U.S.C. 45(a), 52] — Count II, Unsubstantiated Weight Loss Claims

expected_findings.claim: Over the course of the program, eligible customers can expect to lose up to an average of 23% of body weight.
expected_findings.rule: FTC Act §§5(a) and 12 [15 U.S.C. 45(a), 52] — Count II, Unsubstantiated Weight Loss Claims

expected_findings.claim: Monthly prescription to a GLP-1a medication for weight-loss…
expected_findings.rule: FTC Act §5(a) [15 U.S.C. 45(a)] — Count I, Deceptive Cost Claims; Count V, Deceptive Failure to Disclose (¶32: 'an inconspicuous small-print disclaimer' that medication and lab costs were not included)

expected_findings.claim: $99 Ozempic Buy Now - No Diet or Exercise Required
expected_findings.rule: FTC Act §5(a) [15 U.S.C. 45(a)] — Count I, Deceptive Cost Claims (price did not include the GLP-1 drug, labs, or required consultations)

notes: FTC administrative complaint, In the Matter of Southern Health Solutions, Inc. d/b/a Next Medical and NextMed, Robert S. Epstein and Frank Pat Leonardo III (FTC File No. 232-3040); announced with proposed consent order ($150,000) in FTC press release July 14, 2025 (https://www.ftc.gov/node/88624). Quotes come from the complaint: ad copy from ¶16.B–16.H (paid search ad image in ¶16.C, homepage ¶16.F, FAQ ¶16.H) and ¶32 (program graphic); testimonials are verbatim from the website screenshots reproduced in ¶21 (page 13), checked against the rendered page image. Per ¶22, 'Chastity'/'Becky' photos came from Craigslist respondents, 'Pam' is Epstein's mother, and 'Frank' is respondent Leonardo; none used the program. Count II (¶46–47): no records of member weight loss, and ads claimed 'no diet or exercise' while the trials included diet and exercise. Counts IV (unfair review practices: fake Trustpilot reviews, gift cards to change negative reviews), VI–VIII (unauthorized charges, cancellation, EFTA/Reg E) are not ad-copy issues and are not mapped. The TV voiceover 'NextMed offers new FDA approved weight-loss medications like Ozempic and Wegovy' (¶16.B) refers to FDA-approved branded drugs; the complaint cites that ad only for its 'only $99' cost impression (Count I), so it should not be flagged as false_fda_approval_claim. The inadequate_disclosure_prominence mapping is about cost/material-term disclosures, not risk information.

title: Hims & Hers compounded topical finasteride/minoxidil: 'doctor-trusted', 'dermatologist-recommended', safety and side-effect claims
ad_content:
Finasteride is doctor trusted to give even better results when paired with minoxidil, which helps to kickstart regrowth
doctor-trusted ingredients
Hims Hair Hybrids contain a combination of dermatologist-recommended prescription ingredients.
The product is a prescription medication used for the treatment of male pattern hair loss (androgenetic alopecia). It is a treatment alternative to oral finasteride that has been shown in research studies to be safe and effective
[systemic side effects associated with oral finasteride were] “not reported” [in the studies of topical finasteride]

expected_findings.claim: doctor-trusted ingredients
expected_findings.rule: NAD reasonable-basis substantiation standard (BBB National Programs NAD decision; no statute cited) — survey of 250 dermatologists 'not a good fit' for unqualified claim; NAD recommended modifying to clearly and conspicuously disclose survey results

expected_findings.claim: Hims Hair Hybrids contain a combination of dermatologist-recommended prescription ingredients.
expected_findings.rule: NAD reasonable-basis substantiation standard (BBB National Programs NAD decision; no statute cited) — dermatologist-trust survey does not substantiate a dermatologist-recommended claim; NAD recommended discontinuing

expected_findings.claim: Finasteride is doctor trusted to give even better results when paired with minoxidil
expected_findings.rule: NAD reasonable-basis substantiation standard (BBB National Programs NAD decision; no statute cited) — no evidence doctors trust finasteride for that reason; NAD recommended removing 'doctor trusted'

expected_findings.claim: It is a treatment alternative to oral finasteride that has been shown in research studies to be safe and effective
expected_findings.rule: NAD reasonable-basis substantiation standard (BBB National Programs NAD decision; no statute cited) — recommended further modification to avoid conveying that the compounded Hims Spray and Serum were shown safe in clinical studies

expected_findings.claim: not reported
expected_findings.rule: NAD reasonable-basis substantiation standard (BBB National Programs NAD decision; no statute cited) — recommended modifying to avoid implying that systemic side effects associated with finasteride are immaterial or not relevant to consumers

must_not_flag: even better results when paired with minoxidil, which helps to kickstart regrowth
notes: NAD Case #7543 (challenger Kenvue Inc.), BBB National Programs decision summary dated August 24, 2026. Products: Hims Topical Finasteride & Minoxidil Spray and Serum, Hers Postmenopausal Hair Loss Spray, Hers Hair Blends Postmeno Serum (compounded topicals). All claim text is quoted from the decision summary. The 'not reported' line is NAD's description of the claim with only the quoted words verbatim; Hims had already changed it to 'very limited reports', and NAD asked for further modification. NAD also recommended modifying the most-common-side-effect claims so they don't imply local scalp reactions are the only or primarily minor material risks, with non-local risk categories disclosed 'clearly and conspicuously' and 'in close proximity to the claim'. That is a missing_risk_information/inadequate_disclosure_prominence issue, but the summary does not quote that copy, so it is not a finding here. The 'doctor-trusted'/'dermatologist-recommended' claims are expert-endorsement claims and are mapped to misleading_testimonial_or_results, which is the closest enum value. must_not_flag: NAD found a reasonable basis for the comparative efficacy message (finasteride works better with minoxidil than alone); only the 'doctor trusted' wording was objectionable. Hims agreed to comply.

title: Noom Microdose GLP-1Rx 'A Smaller Dose. A Smarter Start.' implied dose-superiority claim
ad_content: NOOM GLP-1Rx PROGRAM A Smaller Dose. A Smarter Start. MICRODOSE GLP-1Rx STARTS AT $119*

expected_findings.claim: A Smaller Dose. A Smarter Start.
expected_findings.rule: NAD reasonable-basis substantiation standard (BBB National Programs NAD decision; no statute cited) — an objective health-related message, not puffery: the 'smaller' dose makes it 'smarter', a better way to begin treatment; recommended discontinuing or modifying

expected_findings.claim: A Smaller Dose. A Smarter Start.
expected_findings.rule: NAD reasonable-basis substantiation standard (BBB National Programs NAD decision; no statute cited) — no adequate support that Noom's lower-dose approach gives a measurable health-related benefit

notes: NAD Case #7539 (challenger Eli Lilly and Company), BBB National Programs decision summary dated May 26, 2026. The claim is quoted verbatim from the decision paragraph that recommends discontinuing it. The summary also gives it as 'Noom GLP-1Rx Program A Smaller Dose. A Smarter Start. Microdose GLP-1Rx Starts at $119*.' The price was not at issue; NAD's concern was the message that the lower dose itself has a measurable health benefit. NAD said Noom can still promote its program or behavior-modification tools as a 'smarter start' if that isn't tied to unsupported dosage benefits. Noom permanently discontinued all other challenged claims (dosing, efficacy, side effect, health) during the inquiry, but the summary doesn't quote them. Noom disagreed but agreed to comply.

title: Altru Telehealth: 'FDA approved' compounding pharmacy and 'same results at a fraction of the cost' claims for compounded GLP-1s
company: Altru Telehealth, LLC dba Altru Telehealth
ad_content:
Compounded semaglutide combines the FDA approved active ingredient semaglutide with a body safe vitamin such as B12.
Compounded semaglutide & tirzepatide offers the same results but at a fraction of the cost of brand names such as Ozempic, Mounjaro & Wegovy.
Semaglutide & Tirzepatide is the active ingredient used in FDA-Approved weekly injection Wegovy® and Mounjaro….
[a]n FDA approved, regulated & sterile compounding pharmacy mixes the formula based on the medical providers [sic] prescription
[o]ur compounding pharmacies are all FDA approved....

expected_findings.claim: Compounded semaglutide combines the FDA approved active ingredient semaglutide with a body safe vitamin such as B12.
Compounded semaglutide & tirzepatide offers the same results but at a fraction of the cost of brand names such as Ozempic, Mounjaro & Wegovy.
Semaglutide & Tirzepatide is the active ingredient used in FDA-Approved weekly injection Wegovy® and Mounjaro….
[a]n FDA approved, regulated & sterile compounding pharmacy mixes the formula based on the medical providers [sic] prescription
[o]ur compounding pharmacies are all FDA approved....

notes: FDA CDER warning letter MARCS-CMS 728274 dated June 8, 2026, from FDA's review of https://altrutelehealth.com in March 2026 (part of the June 2026 telehealth batch). The first three claims are verbatim from item 1 ('The following claims concerning compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide products appear on your website:'). FDA's reasoning: 'Compounded drug products are not FDA-approved. Your claims represent that the compounded drug products you offer have been FDA-approved or otherwise evaluated for safety and effectiveness when they have not.' The two pharmacy claims are verbatim from item 2, with FDA's bracket edits and [sic] kept. FDA says compounding facilities are not 'FDA-approved' or 'FDA-licensed' entities. Mapping: the 'same results … fraction of the cost' claim asserts outcome equivalence with branded drugs plus a price comparison, so it is unsubstantiated_comparative_claim; the 'active ingredient used in FDA-Approved … Wegovy' claim is a sameness claim, so it is compounded_drug_misrepresentation.

title: Ozempic DTC online video 'Ozempic vs. – Random Guy': implied superiority over other GLP-1s, broadened indication, risk info after an end-of-ad signal
ad_content:
Music/SUPER: “There’s Only One Ozempic. O, O, O.”
VO (Stan): “Hm. Now it says here… for adults with type 2 diabetes, Ozempic is the GLP-1 with the most FDA-approved uses” (00:14)
SUPER: “Ozempic® is the GLP-1 with the most FDA-approved uses for adults with type 2 diabetes.”
VO (Stan): “Ozempic is approved to lower A1C . . . ” (00:26)
SUPER: “Ozempic® is proven to lower A1C, along with diet and exercise.”
VO (Stan): “. . . lower the risk of major cardiovascular events like stroke, heart attack, or death . . . ” (00:30)
SUPER: “Ozempic® lowers the risk of major cardiovascular events such as stroke, heart attack, or death in adults with type 2 diabetes and known heart disease.”
VO (Stan): “. . . and lower the risk of worsening chronic kidney disease. Alright, back to you Ozempic.” (00:39)
SUPER: “Ozempic® reduces the risk of kidney disease worsening, kidney failure (end-stage kidney disease), and death due to cardiovascular disease in adults with type 2 diabetes and known chronic kidney disease.”
VO (“Ozempic”): “Thanks Stan.” (00:45)
VO (“other GLP-1s”): “Yeah, cool. Uh, do me next.” (00:47)
VO (Stan): “Well, I see you don’t have as many FDA-approved uses as Ozempic.” (00:49)
VO (“other GLP-1s”): “Oh, really? Well, can Ozempic do this?” [bird-calling sound] (00:53 - 1:01)
VO (“Ozempic”): “Cool. What was that?” (1:02)
VO (“other GLP-1s”): “It was a brown sicklebill.” (1:03)
VO (“Ozempic”): “Right. And that’s a real bird?” (1:06)
VO: Music: “There’s Only One Ozempic . . . ” (1:07) [followed by risk information]

expected_findings.claim: for adults with type 2 diabetes, Ozempic is the GLP-1 with the most FDA-approved uses
expected_findings.rule: FD&C Act misbranding (OPDP untitled letter; no section number cited in letter text) — implies all T2D patients are candidates for all indications; the CV and CKD indications require established cardiovascular disease or chronic kidney disease

expected_findings.claim: Ozempic® is the GLP-1 with the most FDA-approved uses for adults with type 2 diabetes.
expected_findings.rule: FD&C Act misbranding (OPDP untitled letter; no section number cited in letter text) — 'claims and presentations that misrepresent the efficacy of Ozempic'

expected_findings.claim: Well, I see you don’t have as many FDA-approved uses as Ozempic.
expected_findings.rule: FD&C Act misbranding (OPDP untitled letter; no section number cited in letter text) — frames Ozempic as superior to other GLP-1s; the supporting trials were placebo-controlled, not designed to show superiority

expected_findings.claim: There’s Only One Ozempic
expected_findings.rule: FD&C Act misbranding (OPDP untitled letter; no section number cited in letter text) — part of the implied superiority over other GLP-1s, together with the bird-call gag and the orange vs. gray shirts

expected_findings.claim: There’s Only One Ozempic . . .
expected_findings.rule: FD&C Act misbranding (OPDP untitled letter; no section number cited in letter text) — the end-of-ad jingle and logo signal the close, with no cue that important risk information follows

expected_findings.claim: There’s Only One Ozempic . . .
expected_findings.rule: FD&C Act misbranding (OPDP untitled letter; no section number cited in letter text) — presenting risk this way 'misleadingly minimizes the risks associated with the use of Ozempic'; the 'Ozempic-pi.com' PI link at the top of the video does not cure it

must_not_flag: Ozempic® is proven to lower A1C, along with diet and exercise.
Ozempic® lowers the risk of major cardiovascular events such as stroke, heart attack, or death in adults with type 2 diabetes and known heart disease.

Ozempic® reduces the risk of kidney disease worsening, kidney failure (end-stage kidney disease), and death due to cardiovascular disease in adults with type 2 diabetes and known chronic kidney disease.
notes: FDA OPDP untitled letter to Novo Nordisk Inc., RE: NDA 209637 OZEMPIC (semaglutide) injection, MA 1457, Reference ID 5753506, signed February 26, 2026 (listed on FDA's OPDP Untitled Letters page under 2/26/2026). Subject: DTC online video 'Ozempic vs. – Random Guy OLV' (US25OZM01130), submitted on Form FDA 2253. All VO/SUPER text and timestamps are verbatim from pages 1–3 of the letter; the timestamps are FDA's, not verified against video. I couldn't find a public copy of this cut: the YouTube spots in the same Justin Long/John Hodgman campaign that I found had different scripts, so modality is text and timestamp_s is null. The letter cites no CFR or USC section. The off_label_promotion mapping covers OPDP's broadening-of-indication finding: the claim promotes CV and CKD risk reduction to T2D patients outside the labeled populations. The visual superiority cue (Ozempic in a bright orange shirt, 'other GLP-1s' in a dull gray shirt) is cited by the letter but has no verbatim text. must_not_flag: OPDP acknowledges the full indications are shown in these SUPERs; they are accurate indication statements, but they do not cure the misleading VO. Vertical is other_rx because the ad promotes type 2 diabetes indications, not weight loss.

title: Wegovy pill 'January 2026 Pill Spot' TV ad: implied superiority over other GLP-1s, 'live lighter' benefits, non-dual-modality major statement
ad_content:
VO: “Meet Wegovy pill.” ON-SCREEN TEXT: “Meet Wegovy® pill”
VO: “The first and only FDA approved GLP-1 weight loss pill.” ON-SCREEN TEXT: “Only GLP-1 weight-loss pill”
VO: “Weight loss has never looked like this.”
VO: “Now you can live lighter by losing weight.” ON-SCREEN TEXT: “LIVE LIGHTER™ by losing weight”
VO: “The power of Wegovy, now in the palm of your hand.”
VO: “Weight loss with Wegovy isn’t a shortcut. It’s a way forward.”
VO: “Live lighter by losing weight and keeping it off.” ON-SCREEN TEXT: “LIVE LIGHTER™ by losing weight and keeping it off”

expected_findings.claim: Weight loss has never looked like this.
expected_findings.rule: FD&C Act misbranding (OPDP untitled letter; no section number cited in letter text) — the totality implies the pill gives superior efficacy and/or safety over other approved GLP-1s; FDA knows of no supporting data (the PI cites a placebo-controlled trial)

expected_findings.claim: The power of Wegovy, now in the palm of your hand.
expected_findings.rule: FD&C Act misbranding (OPDP untitled letter; no section number cited in letter text) — implies the pill form is an advancement, enabling outcomes not possible with other GLP-1 treatments

expected_findings.claim: LIVE LIGHTER™ by losing weight
expected_findings.rule: FD&C Act misbranding (OPDP untitled letter; no section number cited in letter text) — 'live lighter' implies more weight loss than other GLP-1s and benefits beyond physical weight loss (emotional relief, reduced psychological burden); neither demonstrated

expected_findings.claim: Weight loss with Wegovy isn’t a shortcut. It’s a way forward.
expected_findings.rule: FD&C Act misbranding (OPDP untitled letter; no section number cited in letter text) — 'a way forward' implies hope or direction for patients' lives, presenting the drug as a solution to broader life challenges; not demonstrated

expected_findings.claim: Stop taking and get medical help right away if you get a lump or swelling in your neck, severe stomach pain, or any of these allergic reactions: • Swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat • Problems breathing or swallowing • Severe rash or itching • Fainting or feeling dizzy • Very rapid heartbeat
expected_findings.rule: FD&C Act misbranding (OPDP untitled letter; no section number cited in letter text) — 'the major statement includes presentations where there is information in the SUPERs that is not from the corresponding audio', so it is not presented concurrently in audio and text (dual modality)

expected_findings.claim: Serious side effects may include pancreas inflammation and gallbladder or severe stomach problems. Call your prescriber if you have: • Stomach pain • Fever • Yellowing of the skin or eyes • Clay-colored stools
expected_findings.rule: FD&C Act misbranding (OPDP untitled letter; no section number cited in letter text) — dual modality: SUPER content not in the corresponding audio

must_not_flag: People who stopped taking Wegovy® generally regained weight.
For adults with obesity or excess weight, along with diet and exercise
notes: FDA OPDP untitled letter to Novo Nordisk Inc., RE: NDA 218316 WEGOVY (semaglutide) tablets, MA 6, Reference ID 5740851, signed February 5, 2026. Subject: DTC TV ad 'January 2026 Pill Spot' (US25SEMO01839). Page 1 of the PDF is a scanned image; I rendered and read it. ad_content is the VO/ON-SCREEN TEXT list from page 1, verbatim. The reasoning (implied superiority from the dosage form, 'live lighter'/'a way forward', dual modality) is on page 2. The letter cites no CFR or USC section. Video: a third-party upload, YouTube 'Wegovy Commercial (2026, Golden Globes)' by channel 'Commercial Archivist' (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NrkDMTS56uU, uploaded 2026-01-12, 75 s). Its auto-captions contain every VO line the letter quotes, in the same order, so it is very likely the same spot, but the 2253 ID can't be confirmed from the upload. Timestamps come from caption timing. Frames were extracted and read at 9 s, 36 s, 42 s ('LIVE LIGHTER™ by losing weight' super), 39 s (the allergic-reaction bullets are on screen while the audio says only 'any of these allergic reactions') and 47 s (the 'Call your prescriber if you have:' symptom bullets are on screen while the audio says only 'any of these symptoms'), plus 69 s (closing 'LIVE LIGHTER™ by losing weight and keeping it off'). The letter doesn't say which SUPER lines lack audio; the two dual-modality findings are the on-screen-only lists I observed. 'The first and only FDA approved GLP-1 weight loss pill' is accurate as an approval claim (Wegovy tablets are approved under NDA 218316) and must not be flagged as false_fda_approval_claim. It is part of the 'totality' OPDP cites for the dosage-form superiority implication, so it is left out of must_not_flag. must_not_flag lines are accurate on-screen indication/limitation text read from frames at 2 s and 18 s.
